The major thrust of Marx's political philosophy was aimed at human liberation; it is important to consider the significant shift to comprehend it; the shift occurred in the late 17th century; in that period traditional analysis of the political order based on scarcity was replaced by a philosophy of abundance.
options: Comprehending the major thrust of Marx's political philosophy that was aimed at human liberation, it is important to consider the significant shift of late 17th century when the scarcity based on traditional analysis was replaced by a philosophy of abundance.

Marx's major thrust was on political philosophy aiming human liberation while it is important to consider the significant shift that occurred in the late 17th century, it was then that traditional analysis of the political order based on scarcity was replaced by a philosophy of abundance.

It is important to consider the significant shift in the late 17th century when traditional analysis of the political order based on scarcity replaced philosophy of abundance to comprehend the major thrust of Marx's political philosophy of human liberation.

To comprehend the major thrust of Marx's political philosophy that aimed at human liberation, it is important to consider the significant shift that occurred in the late 17th century when traditional analysis of the political order based on scarcity was replaced by a philosophy of abundance.
None of the above is correct.
questions.explanation: Option (d) is the only version that is both grammatical and faithful: the infinitive of purpose 'To comprehend...' correctly frames why the shift matters, and the relative clause keeps the original direction of replacement (scarcity-based analysis replaced BY a philosophy of abundance). Option (a) garbles that relation ('the scarcity based on traditional analysis'), (b) distorts the subject ('Marx's major thrust was on political philosophy') and splices clauses, and (c) reverses what replaced what. Hence (d).

questions.question:
The sentence below is divided into three parts, one or more of which may contain a grammatical error. From the alternatives (I), (II), (III) given after it, find the correct replacement(s) for the erroneous part(s). If a part is erroneous but no alternative correctly replaces it, choose (d); if the sentence needs no correction, choose (e).

Italian officials have been arguing that (I)/ volatility caused by Britain's vote to leave the European Union (II)/ means it could have given greater flexibility to prop up struggling banks. (III)

(I) Italian officials had argued that
(II) volatility that caused Britain's vote to leave the European Union
(III) meant it should be given greater flexibility to prop up struggling banks
questions.explanation: The sentence needs past-tense consistency: in part (I) 'have been arguing' should become 'had argued', and in part (III) 'means it could have given' should become 'meant it should be given greater flexibility'. Alternative (II) must be rejected because 'volatility that caused Britain's vote' reverses cause and effect — the vote caused the volatility, not the other way round. Hence (b) Both (I) and (III).

questions.question:
A part of the sentence below is given in quotes (bold in the original). Three statements follow that try to explain the meaning of that phrase. Choose the set of statements that explains it correctly without altering the meaning of the sentence.

There are girls in that school; droves and scads of them. Most of them beautiful, some of them not-so-good-looking (because 'ugly' is such an ugly word), but that is "neither here nor there".

[Statements paraphrased from the original]
(I) Most of the girls in the school are not-so-good-looking, but that does not make them different.
(II) There are a large number of girls in that school, most of them beautiful and quite a few not-so-good-looking, but that fact is inconsequential.
(III) While most of the girls in that school are beautiful and some are not-so-good-looking, that makes a big difference.
questions.explanation: The idiom 'neither here nor there' means of no importance or relevance. Statement (II) keeps both the facts (many girls; most beautiful, some not) and the idiom's sense — the looks are 'inconsequential', i.e. not important. Statement (I) flips the quantifier (claiming most are not-so-good-looking) and muddles the conclusion, while (III) asserts the looks 'make a big difference', the exact opposite of the idiom. Hence (b) Only (II).

questions.question:
Each of the two statements below has two blanks. Choose the option providing the pair of words that fits both blanks in both statements, in the same order, making them meaningful and grammatically correct.

(1) The molecular targeting of CSCs may improve the ________ of current chemotherapeutic ________ needed for the management of this disease.
(2) ________ and safety of once-daily ________ in the treatment of HIV infection is currently under inspection.
questions.explanation: 'Efficacy, regimens' fits both statements. Efficacy means the ability to produce a desired or intended result — one improves the efficacy of chemotherapy and tests the efficacy and safety of an HIV treatment. Regimen means a prescribed course of medical treatment, diet or exercise — 'chemotherapeutic regimens' and 'once-daily regimens' are the natural collocations. Pairs like 'emasculation, nutriments' or 'sufficiency, subsistence' are meaningless in these medical contexts. Hence (b).

questions.question:
An inference is given in quotes (bold in the original), followed by three statements. Find the statement(s) from which it can be inferred and choose the option with the best possible outcome.

Inference: "Country's economic standard can be best adjudged by per capita income."

[Statements condensed from the original]
(I) Exports and imports, a swelling favourable balance of trade, investments and bank balances are not an index of national prosperity: England exported noticeably more before the Second World War than it does today, yet enjoys greater national prosperity now because the income of average Englishmen — field and factory labourers, clerks, policemen, petty shopkeepers, domestic and other low-paid workers — has gone up.
(II) Per capita real income can be rising even while per capita consumption of goods and services falls — as when the government itself uses up the increased income on a massive military build-up requiring heavy production of arms and ammunition.
(III) National income may rise merely because of increased spending on items such as defence; in war or the threat of war, weapons spending pushes up GNP even though people may be acutely short of goods to buy.
questions.explanation: Statement (I) supports the inference: it dismisses trade balances, investments and bank balances as measures of prosperity and credits England's greater prosperity to the risen income of the average person — i.e., per capita income is the true gauge. Statement (II) conflicts with the inference, showing per capita income rising while actual consumption falls, and statement (III) is about national income/GNP giving a distorted picture, not about per capita income being the best measure. Hence (c) Only (I).

questions.question:
Four statements are given below. Choose the option that connects them into a single sentence which is both grammatically correct and contextually meaningful, without altering their meaning. If none does, choose (e).

There is a giant footprint of the ransomware attack; it leveraged a leaked NSA-created Windows hacking technique; it infected more than 200,000 systems across 150 countries; malware analysts say poor choices on the part of WannaCry's creators have limited both its scope and profit.
options: The giant footprint of the ransomware attack has leveraged a leaked NSA-created Windows hacking technique and infected more than 200,000 systems across 150 countries while malware analysts say poor choices on the part of WannaCry's creators had limited both its scope and profit.

Despite the giant footprint of the ransomware attack, which leveraged a leaked NSA-created Windows hacking technique to infect more than 200,000 systems across 150 countries, malware analysts say poor choices on the part of WannaCry's creators have limited both its scope and profit.

Malware analysts said that poor choices on the part of WannaCry's creators have limited both its scope and profit, whereas the giant footprint of the ransomware attack leveraged a leaked NSA-created Windows hacking technique infecting more than 200,000 systems across 150 countries.

The ransomware attack is a giant footprint as it has leveraged a leaked NSA-created Windows hacking technique and infected more than 200,000 systems across 150 countries which have limited both the scope and profit due to poor choices on the part of WannaCry's creators as malware analysts said.
None of the above is correct.
questions.explanation: Option (b) is the only grammatically sound and logically faithful combination: 'Despite the giant footprint... which leveraged... to infect...' correctly subordinates the attack's scale, against which the analysts' point about limited scope and profit stands in contrast. Option (a) makes the 'footprint' itself the agent that leveraged and infected, (c) sets up a false 'whereas' contrast and shifts tense, and (d) absurdly calls the attack 'a giant footprint' and tangles the final clauses. Hence (b).

questions.question:
The sentence below is divided into three parts, one or more of which may contain a grammatical error. From the alternatives (I), (II), (III) given after it, find the correct replacement(s) for the erroneous part(s). If a part is erroneous but no alternative correctly replaces it, choose (d); if the sentence needs no correction, choose (e).

Many environmentalists think that too much interference with (I)/ nature for development projects is gradually destroying the balance and natural (II)/ calamities are happening to forewarn us about a possible doomsday in future. (III)

(I) Many of the environmentalists believe that too much interference in
(II) nature for developing new projects has destroyed the balance and natural
(III) calamities which may happen to forewarn us about doomsday possibly in future
questions.explanation: The sentence is grammatically correct as it stands: 'interference with nature' is the right collocation, the present continuous 'is gradually destroying' suits an ongoing process, and 'calamities are happening to forewarn us' is a valid coordinate clause. Each proposed alternative would actually damage the sentence — 'interference in', the perfect 'has destroyed' against 'gradually', and the fragment 'calamities which may happen...' that leaves the second clause without a main verb. Hence (e) No correction required.

questions.question:
Each of the two statements below has two blanks. Choose the option providing the pair of words that fits both blanks in both statements, in the same order, making them meaningful and grammatically correct.

(1) The six-day war was the last unalloyed military victory for Israel, and the start of a ________ from existential wars against Arab states, which it always won, to ________ campaigns against non-state militias which it could never wipe out.
(2) He sees these dualities as having been maintained through the ________ by a deliberate and ________ general amnesia.
questions.explanation: 'Transition, enervating' fits both statements. Transition means the process or period of changing from one state to another — a shift from existential wars to a different kind of campaign, and dualities maintained 'through the transition'. Enervating means draining of energy or vitality — apt for wearying campaigns against militias that could never be wiped out, and for a deliberate, sapping general amnesia. 'Invigorating' and 'exhilarating' convey the opposite sense, and 'enfeeble' is the wrong form (a verb where an adjective is needed). Hence (a).

questions.question:
A small paragraph is given, followed by three possible inferences which may or may not be correct. Choose the option which gives the best possible outcome.

[Paragraph condensed from the original]
Techniques that raise productivity in discrete tasks by requiring less human labour at each step of the production process are widely used. Productivity consultants point out, however, that although these techniques achieve their specific goal, they are not without drawbacks: they often breed enough resentment in the workforce eventually to cause a slowdown in the production process as a whole.

(I) The fact that productivity enhancement techniques are so widely employed has led to a decline in the ability of American business to compete abroad.
(II) Productivity enhancement techniques do not attain their intended purpose and should not be employed in the workplace.
(III) Ironically, an increase in the productivity of discrete tasks may result in a decrease in the productivity of the whole production process.
options: None of the given inferences is correct.
questions.explanation: Only inference (III) follows: the paragraph says the techniques boost productivity at individual steps yet the resentment they cause can eventually slow the production process as a whole — precisely the irony (III) states. (I) introduces foreign competitiveness of American business, which the paragraph never mentions, and (II) contradicts the paragraph, which concedes the techniques 'achieve their specific goal'. Hence (c) Only (III).

questions.question:
Each of the two statements below has two blanks. Choose the option providing the pair of words that fits both blanks in both statements, in the same order, making them meaningful and grammatically correct.

(1) The obvious ________ between China's level of participation and other Asian states' requires some ________.
(2) For years there has been talk Aldo's lazy performances had more to do with a brutal weight cut than any skill ________. That's always been a pretty probable ________, given the number of horrendous weight cuts MMA sees.
questions.explanation: 'Discrepancy, explanation' fits both statements. Discrepancy means an illogical or surprising lack of compatibility between facts — apt for the gap between China's participation and other Asian states', and for a skill discrepancy behind lazy performances. An obvious discrepancy 'requires some explanation', and a weight-cut theory being 'a pretty probable explanation' reads naturally, whereas 'delineation', 'cogitation', 'contemplation' and 'rumination' do not fit the second blank in either statement. Hence (b).

questions.question:
Four statements are given below. Choose the option that connects them into a single sentence which is both grammatically correct and contextually meaningful, without altering their meaning. If none does, choose (e).

Pro-Russian hackers bombarded the sites of opposition leaders; it included Garry Kasparov in the midst of his 2007 campaign for president; it started in the late 2000s; it kept Kasparov's site offline or sluggish at key moments during the campaign season.
options: Bombarding the sites of opposition leaders including Garry Kasparov the midst of his 2007 campaign for president in the late 2000s, Kasparov's site was kept offline or sluggish at key moments during the campaigning season.

In the late 2000s, pro-Russian hackers started bombarding the sites of opposition leaders that included Garry Kasparov in the midst of his 2007 campaign for president and keeping Kasparov's site offline or sluggish at key moments during the campaign season.

Starting in the late 2000s, pro-Russian hackers bombarded the sites of opposition leaders like Garry Kasparov in the midst of his 2007 campaign for president, keeping Kasparov's site offline or sluggish at key moments during the campaign season.

The sites of opposition leaders like Garry Kasparov was kept offline or sluggish at key moments during the campaigning season by pro-Russian hackers who bombarded the sites in the midst of his 2007 campaign for President.
None of the above is correct.
questions.explanation: Option (c) is grammatically clean and preserves every fact: 'Starting in the late 2000s' fixes the time, the hackers are the clear subject of 'bombarded', and the participial 'keeping Kasparov's site offline or sluggish' correctly attaches the result. Option (a) is a dangling modifier (it makes Kasparov's site the bomber), (b) awkwardly coordinates 'started bombarding... and keeping', and (d) has faulty agreement ('The sites... was kept'). Hence (c).

questions.question:
The sentence below is divided into three parts, one or more of which may contain a grammatical error. From the alternatives (I), (II), (III) given after it, find the correct replacement(s) for the erroneous part(s). If a part is erroneous but no alternative correctly replaces it, choose (d); if the sentence needs no correction, choose (e).

Career diplomats in the State Department are wringing (I)/ the hands of diplomats in despair after seeing their president (II)/ uncorking US policies which had taken decades at maturing. (III)

(I) Diplomacy in Career in the State Department has wringed
(II) their hands in despair at seeing their president
(III) uncorking US policies that have taken decades to mature
questions.explanation: Part (II) should read 'their hands in despair at seeing their president' — the diplomats wring their own hands, and 'at seeing' is the correct phrase, not 'after seeing'. Part (III) should be 'that have taken decades to mature', keeping the present-tense frame and the correct infinitive instead of 'which had taken decades at maturing'. Part (I) is already correct, and its proposed alternative ('Diplomacy in Career... has wringed') is gibberish. Hence (a) Both (II) and (III).

questions.question:
An inference is given in quotes (bold in the original), followed by three statements. Find the statement(s) from which it can be inferred and choose the option with the best possible outcome.

Inference: "GDP fluctuates because of the business cycle."

[Statements condensed from the original]
(I) The downturn of a business cycle is called a recession, defined as a period in which real GDP declines for at least two consecutive quarters; a recession begins at a peak and ends at a trough, after which conditions improve and the economy gradually enters the expansionary phase.
(II) As interest rates rise, companies and consumers cut back spending and the economy slows; slowing demand leads companies to lay off employees, further denting consumer confidence and demand, until the central bank eases monetary policy to stimulate growth and employment and the economy booms once again — and the cycle repeats.
(III) A high share of investment in GDP may be superb for creating extra productive capacity, but it comes at the expense of consumer goods and services for the current generation — an imbalance that is one reason GDP data may give a distorted picture of living standards in a country.
questions.explanation: Per the book's key, only statement (II) yields the inference: it traces the self-repeating loop — rate rises, spending cuts, layoffs, then monetary easing and a fresh boom — that drives the economy, and hence GDP, up and down. Statement (I) merely defines and labels the phases of the cycle rather than showing GDP fluctuating because of it, and statement (III) concerns GDP as a distorted measure of living standards, not its fluctuation. Hence (d) Only (II).

questions.question:
Each of the two statements below has two blanks. Choose the option providing the pair of words that fits both blanks in both statements, in the same order, making them meaningful and grammatically correct.

(1) Polish environment minister to ________ over COP24 conference, the choice was made ________ by the climate-change committee of the United Nations.
(2) The Labour Party is led by two Marxists: Mr Corbyn and John McDonnell, his shadow chancellor, who believe in the materialist interpretation of history. Yet they now ________ over a coalition of voters defined ________ by their shared values.
questions.explanation: 'Preside, overwhelmingly' fits both statements. Preside means to be in the position of authority in a meeting or gathering — one presides over a conference, and party leaders preside over a coalition of voters. Overwhelmingly means to a very great degree or by a great majority — a choice made overwhelmingly by the UN committee, and voters defined overwhelmingly by shared values. 'Debate over', 'concoct over' and 'conduct over' fail the idiom, since 'preside' is the only verb that takes 'over' naturally in both contexts. Hence (e).

questions.question:
An inference is given in quotes (bold in the original), followed by three statements. Find the statement(s) from which it can be inferred and choose the option with the best possible outcome.

Inference: "The calorie count of foods that are high in carbohydrates is significant."

[Statements condensed from the original]
(I) Moderate use of non-nutritive sweeteners like aspartame for a low calorie count could help weight control and so benefit insulin and blood sugar; still, many foods containing aspartame provide calories and carbohydrate from other ingredients even though they may be labelled 'sugar-free'.
(II) Ironically, people who use aspartame as a sweetener to cut their calorie intake could wind up defeating their purpose, since studies show high levels of aspartame may trigger a craving for carbohydrates by depleting the brain of a chemical that registers carbohydrate satiety.
(III) The Institute of Medicine recommends that 45 to 65 percent of total calories come from carbs; with regular carb consumption, glycogen stores stay full and become a normal part of total body weight, and aspartame's rise in popularity is due to its comparatively low calorie count.
questions.explanation: Statements (I) and (II) both build on the premise that carbohydrate calories matter: (I) warns that 'sugar-free' aspartame products still deliver calories and carbohydrate from other ingredients, and (II) shows calorie-cutting via aspartame backfiring through carbohydrate cravings — each treating the calorie count of carbohydrate-rich food as significant. Statement (III) recommends a share of calories from carbs but never indicates that carbohydrate-rich foods are significantly caloric. Hence (c) Both (I) and (II).

questions.question:
Four statements are given below. Choose the option that connects them into a single sentence which is both grammatically correct and contextually meaningful, without altering their meaning. If none does, choose (e).

Hong Kong has prospered economically; it is visible from US $177 billion GDP in 1997 to $319 billion; it has risen by 80 per cent; it has been building on her strengths of superior infrastructure, free port and low-tax status, and her superior financial and logistic hubs.
options: Economically, Hong Kong has prospered visibly, from US $177 billion GDP in 1997 to $319 billion, rising by 80 per cent, building on her strengths of superior infrastructure, free port and low-tax status, and her superior financial and logistic hubs.

Hong Kong has been prospering economically which is visible from US $177 billion GDP in 1997 to $319 billion that has risen by 80 per cent which has been building on her strengths of superior infrastructure, free port and low-tax status, and her superior financial and logistic hubs.

Building on her strengths of superior infrastructure, free port and low-tax status, and her superior financial and logistic hubs, Hong Kong has prospered economically visible from US $177 billion GDP in 1997 to $319 billion that has risen by 80 per cent.

Hong Kong has made visibly a prosperous economic condition rising by 80 per cent from US $177 billion GDP in 1997 to $319 billion which shows that it has been building on her strengths of superior infrastructure, free port and low-tax status, and her superior financial and logistic hubs.
None of the above is correct.
questions.explanation: Option (a) strings all four facts into one clean sentence: the prosperity is stated first, the GDP movement and the 80 per cent rise sit as neat appositive phrases, and the participial 'building on her strengths...' supplies the cause. Option (b) chains 'which... that... which' into an ungrammatical tangle, (c) misattaches 'visible' and 'that has risen', and (d) distorts the meaning ('has made visibly a prosperous economic condition') and reverses the logic with 'which shows that'. Hence (a).

questions.question:
The sentence below is divided into three parts, one or more of which may contain a grammatical error. From the alternatives (I), (II), (III) given after it, find the correct replacement(s) for the erroneous part(s). If a part is erroneous but no alternative correctly replaces it, choose (d); if the sentence needs no correction, choose (e).

Around 1960s it was widely assumed about politics which had been (I)/ divided from religions and after societies started becoming more industrialized, religious (II)/ belief and practice were restricted to private thought and action. (III)

(I) Politics was assumed widely till about 1960s that it is
(II) divided out of religion and as societies were becoming more industrialized, religious
(III) beliefs and practices should have restricted to private thoughts and actions.
questions.explanation: All three parts of the sentence are faulty, but none of the offered alternatives repairs them: (I) 'Politics was assumed widely... that it is' is itself ungrammatical, (II) 'divided out of religion' is the wrong idiom, and (III) 'should have restricted' lacks the required passive. The book gives the corrected sentence as: 'Till about the 1960s it was widely assumed that politics was divided from religion and that as societies became more industrialized, religious belief and practice would be restricted to private thought and action.' Hence (d) None of the (I), (II) and (III).

questions.question:
A part of the sentence below is given in quotes (bold in the original). Three statements follow that try to explain the meaning of that phrase. Choose the set of statements that explains it correctly without altering the meaning of the sentence.

Having studied the laws of social development and of capitalism, Marx sought to prove that the destruction of capitalism was inevitable, for it had given rise to its "own grave diggers".

[Statements paraphrased from the original]
(I) After studying the laws of social development and of capitalism, Marx was assured that capitalism would be completely destroyed, as the ones who had constructed it would themselves be responsible for its downfall.
(II) The laws of social development and of capitalism were so deplorable that Marx felt they would destroy capitalism, and that it would soon give rise to a new destructive method.
(III) Marx's studies suggested that the laws of social development and capitalism were so woeful that the desolation of capitalism was certain, and nothing other than these laws themselves would be accountable for its destruction.
questions.explanation: The phrase adapts the idiom 'digging one's own grave' — doing something unwise that brings about one's own downfall: capitalism itself produced the forces that would destroy it. Statement (III) captures this — the workings of capitalism's own laws, and nothing external, would be accountable for its destruction. Statement (I) wrongly pins the downfall on capitalism's constructors, and (II) invents a 'new destructive method'. Hence (c) Only (III). Note: the book misprints both options (b) and (c) as 'Only (III)'; per the answer key (c) and the solution, (b) has been restored here to the evidently intended 'Only (II) is correct'.

questions.question:
If Sentence (C), "Presidential contests in India are usually tame and predictable, and 2017 does not promise to be any different" is the first sentence, what is the order of the other sentences after rearrangement?

(A) Prime Minister Indira Gandhi called for a "conscience vote" just before the election, and a sizeable number of Congress parliamentarians and legislators voted against the "official" candidate, Reddy, in favour of Giri.
(B) The Bharatiya Janata Party, with its regular allies and new-found friends, should be able to see any non-controversial candidate through.
(C) Presidential contests in India are usually tame and predictable, and 2017 does not promise to be any different.
(D) To date, the election of V.V. Giri over Neelam Sanjiva Reddy in 1969 remains the only notable exception to the long list of humdrum presidential elections.
(E) Before and after that, however, the favourites have carried the day, with opposition-sponsored candidates putting up no more than a symbolic fight to prove no more than a political point.
(F) At present, the numbers are stacked against the opposition for the July 17 election.
questions.explanation: After C's claim that presidential contests are tame, D naturally follows by citing the only notable exception — Giri's win over Reddy in 1969; A then details that exception (Indira Gandhi's 'conscience vote' and the Congress cross-voting); E steps back to note that before and after that episode the favourites have always carried the day; F brings the discussion to the present, with numbers stacked against the opposition for the July 17 election; and B concludes that the BJP and its allies can see any non-controversial candidate through. The order is DAEFB, hence (c).

questions.question:
If sentence (C), "The IS immediately claimed responsibility for the attack that killed 12 people" is the last sentence of the paragraph, then which of the following sentences does not fit into the paragraph formed after rearranging the other sentences?

(A) The terrorists clearly wanted to send a message to the Iranian state, and they retained the element of surprise.
(B) The attack, the first major terror incident in Iran in many years, suggests that even the formidable security cover put in place by the elite Revolutionary Guards can be breached by terrorists.
(C) The IS immediately claimed responsibility for the attack that killed 12 people.
(D) But the attacks and the Iranian reaction must also be seen in the context of heightened Saudi Arabia-Iran rivalry.
(E) Wednesday's attacks in Tehran targeted the two most significant symbols of the 1979 Revolution — the Parliament and the tomb of Ayatollah Khomeini, the founder of the Islamic Republic.
(F) Though it is involved in the fight against the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria, Iran has so far largely remained insulated from the regional crises.
questions.explanation: With C fixed as the last sentence, the coherent paragraph is EAFBC: E introduces Wednesday's attacks on the two symbols of the 1979 Revolution; A explains the attackers' intent and element of surprise; F notes that Iran, despite fighting the IS in Iraq and Syria, had largely stayed insulated from regional crises; B observes that this first major terror incident in years shows even the Revolutionary Guards' security cover can be breached; and C closes with the IS claiming responsibility. Sentence (D), on the Saudi Arabia-Iran rivalry, is unrelated to this narrative and does not fit. Hence (d).
